unit.title: Shortest and best: puzzles, paths, packing

lesson.title: Puzzles with rules
lesson.subtitle: Cross out what can’t be, and guess only when you’re stuck

video.title: Puzzles with rules
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Ms Salma Haddad — your maths teacher (main character)
Mr Joseph Mwangi — your computer studies teacher (cameo)
Narrator — the Darsi voice (warm, talks to the student)

scenes.visual: Ms Salma holds up a 4 × 4 sudoku on a card; a few numbers are filled in.
scenes.animation: The grid draws itself; given numbers pop in.
scenes.narration: Here’s a puzzle with four rows and four columns. Every row, every column and every box must have the numbers one to four, once each. Where do you start?

scenes.visual: Title card with the Darsi mark and the Optimization track chip.
scenes.animation: Mark pops in; title slides up.
scenes.narration: Today: puzzles with rules, and how rules save guesses.

scenes.visual: A row, a column and a 2 × 2 box light up in turn.
scenes.animation: Each part glows as it is named.
scenes.narration: This puzzle is called a sudoku. The rule is simple: no number twice in a row, a column or a box. Some numbers are given to start you off.

scenes.visual: Small numbers 1 2 3 4 in one square; three of them get crossed out, one by one.
scenes.narration: For an empty square, think of every number that could go there: one, two, three or four. Then cross out every number already in its row, its column and its box. What’s left are its candidates.

scenes.visual: A square with one candidate left turns into a big number; that number disappears from the small numbers around it.
scenes.animation: The big number lands; small copies vanish nearby.
scenes.narration: Sometimes only one candidate is left. Then that square is solved, for sure. Write it in, and cross it out of its neighbours.

scenes.visual: Mr Joseph points at an empty square; its row shows 1 and 3, its column 4. Three answer cards drop in.
scenes.narration: Quick check! A square’s row already has one and three. Its column has four. What goes in the square?

scenes.visual: The 2 lands in the square; then the whole 4 × 4 grid fills up, square by square.
scenes.narration: Two: it’s the only number left. That’s how rules do the work for you. On a four by four sudoku, crossing out solves the whole puzzle without a single guess.

scenes.visual: A 9 × 9 grid; one square gets a guess in a different colour, then is rubbed out and replaced.
scenes.animation: The guess appears, a red X shows a dead end, an eraser wipes it.
scenes.narration: Big puzzles can get stuck: every empty square still has two or more candidates. Then guess in the square with the fewest, and keep crossing out. If you reach a dead end, undo the guess and try the next one.

scenes.visual: A bar chart: a huge bar for guessing only, a tiny one for crossing out first.
scenes.animation: The big bar shoots up; the tiny bar barely appears.
scenes.narration: A computer that only guesses needed thirteen thousand five hundred and twenty-eight guesses on a hard nine by nine sudoku. Crossing out first, it needed four. That’s why computers that plan school timetables use rules first.

scenes.visual: A school timetable grid with a rule card pinned beside it.
scenes.narration: Timetables have rules just like puzzles: no teacher in two classes at once. They can have fair rules too. For example: nobody always gets the last lesson of the week.

scenes.visual: A phone with the lab: a 4 × 4 grid with small candidates; a finger presses One step.
scenes.on_screen_text: App lab: Sudoku by the rules
scenes.narration: In the app, pick four by four and press One step. Watch the small candidates disappear. Then try a hard nine by nine and count the guesses.

scenes.visual: Ms Salma shows a grid where every empty square has two small numbers. Three answer cards appear.
scenes.narration: Your turn. Every empty square has two candidates left. What do you do?

scenes.visual: Summary lines and an orange takeaway bar.
scenes.animation: Lines tick in; the takeaway slides up.
scenes.narration: Guess in one square, keep crossing out, and undo a guess that leads to a dead end. Remember: rules cross out what can’t be. Only one left? Write it in. And guess only when you’re stuck.

scenes.visual: Two pupils swap paper puzzles across a desk, pencils ready.
scenes.animation: Papers slide across; pencils start crossing out.
scenes.narration: Try it yourself: make a four by four sudoku for a friend, with a few numbers given. Swap puzzles and solve them by crossing out. Did anyone need a guess?

checkpoints.prompt: A square’s row has 1 and 3, and its column has 4. What goes in the square?
checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — 1, 3 and 4 are crossed out, so only 2 is left.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — cross out 1 and 3 (the row) and 4 (the column). Only 2 is left.

checkpoints.prompt: Every empty square has two candidates left. What do you do?

options.text: Give up: it can’t be solved
Guess in one square, keep crossing out, undo if it goes wrong

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — guess where there are fewest candidates, keep crossing out, and undo a guess that leads to a dead end.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — you’re stuck, not beaten. Guess in one square, keep crossing out, and undo the guess if it leads to a dead end.
